title: Choosing among built-in tools, custom tools, Skills, and MCP servers
concept: Claude can be extended in four main ways, and each fits a different kind of need. Built-in tools are capabilities the platform already ships: Claude Code and Agent SDK tools such as Read, Edit, Grep, and Bash, and Anthropic's server-side tools such as web search, web fetch, and code execution. They cost nothing to host and are already integrated with permissions. Custom (client) tools are functions your application defines and executes itself; they suit actions one app owns that depend on its own context, such as the logged-in user's session or a database transaction. Skills package procedural knowledge (instructions, templates, reference files, helper scripts) behind a short description, and the full content loads only when a task calls for it. MCP servers expose tools, resources, and prompts for an external system over a standard protocol, so one independently maintained integration can serve Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Agent SDK apps, and the Messages API connector. A practical order is to start with the built-in tool if it covers the need, use a Skill when the gap is knowledge, use a custom tool when the action is local to one app, and use an MCP server when live access to an external system must be shared. Real systems often combine them, such as an MCP server for Jira plus a Skill for the triage rubric.
why_it_matters: The wrong mechanism costs time and reliability: a hosted server that only returns static text, a scraper that duplicates built-in web search, a CLAUDE.md that loads a rarely used procedure into every session, or duplicated tools across apps that drift. Choosing well keeps context lean, keeps credentials in the right place, and minimizes what the team has to maintain.
common_trap: Defaulting to building something, usually an MCP server, for every need. Static guidance belongs in a Skill, capabilities the platform already ships belong to built-in tools, and an MCP server earns its operational cost when it provides live, shared access to an external system.

title: Framing a business problem for a Claude-based solution
concept: Translating a business problem starts before any model choice. First, narrow a vague ambition ("use AI to grow sales") to a bounded task with an owner, a baseline, and a metric tied to the outcome the business actually cares about. Second, test LLM fit: Claude is strongest where inputs are unstructured language and judgment is needed; exact rules, calculations, lookups, and numeric prediction belong in code or purpose-built models, with Claude handling the language-heavy edges such as extraction and drafting. Third, check feasibility cheaply: confirm the needed data exists and is accessible, then run a small prototype on real labeled samples to learn what accuracy is achievable. Fourth, define success so it cannot be gamed: measure outcomes (resolved without recontact, edit-free acceptance, critical-omission rate) rather than activity (deflection, tokens, usage). Fifth, size scope by risk: segment the work so low-risk, high-volume cases are automated while high-stakes decisions keep human review, and pick a first pilot with a human baseline and recoverable errors. The result is a short statement of what Claude does, what it does not do, how it will be measured, and what must be true for the project to proceed.
why_it_matters: Most failed AI projects fail at framing: the wrong task, an unmeasurable goal, or data that does not exist. Getting framing right makes every later architecture, evaluation, and governance decision easier to justify.
common_trap: Starting from the technology (a model, a general assistant) rather than a measurable task, and using activity metrics that the system can hit without delivering the business outcome.

title: End-to-end architecture: input, processing, output, feedback
concept: An end-to-end Claude architecture has four parts. Input: intake normalizes and screens data (format conversion, size limits, redaction, permission checks) so downstream stages see predictable content. Processing: one or more LLM and code stages, each with a narrow responsibility and a defined output contract, typically a schema; deterministic code owns control flow, lookups, and side effects. Output: results pass through validation (schema, business rules, cross-checks such as totals that must add up) and then a delivery step, with high-risk results routed to human review. Feedback: reviewer corrections, validation failures, and downstream outcomes are captured with their inputs and fed into evaluation sets and prompt or retrieval changes. Failure handling runs through all stages: classify failures (transient, correctable by feedback, source-absent, policy), retry only what a retry can fix, bound retries, persist per-stage state so work resumes instead of restarting, make side-effecting writes idempotent, and escalate what cannot be fixed. Validate at each stage boundary so an error is caught where it is created, and keep a trace so any output can be explained afterwards.
why_it_matters: Production failures rarely come from a single prompt; they come from unvalidated handoffs, missing recovery paths, and loops that never learn. A clear stage and feedback design makes systems debuggable, safe to retry, and improvable.
common_trap: Putting all quality control in a final review step, or retrying every failure the same way. Retries cannot supply data missing from the source, and a late check sees errors only after they have been embedded downstream.

title: Choosing an architectural pattern: augmented LLM, workflow, or agent
concept: Start from the simplest thing that works and add structure only when evaluation shows it helps. The building block is the augmented LLM: one Claude call enhanced with retrieval, tools, or memory. Many problems stop here. When one call is not enough, use a workflow, where code defines the path and Claude fills steps. Prompt chaining suits fixed sequential steps. Routing classifies an input and sends it to a specialized prompt or model. Parallelization runs independent subtasks at once (sectioning) or repeats a task for consensus (voting). Orchestrator-workers lets a model split a task whose subtasks are unknown in advance and delegate them. Evaluator-optimizer loops a generator with a critic when criteria are clear and feedback improves results. Use an agent, where the model chooses its own steps and tools in a loop, only when the path cannot be specified up front, the value justifies higher cost and latency, and mistakes are recoverable. Constraints push back toward workflows: regulatory repeatability, bounded cost, tight latency, and auditability. Real systems are often hybrids, with a routed fast path for common cases and a bounded agent for the long tail. Every step up adds cost, latency, and failure modes, so each needs evidence behind it.
why_it_matters: Pattern choice shapes cost, latency, reliability, and how easily a system can be debugged and audited. Over-building with agents is a common, expensive mistake, and under-building with one prompt fails on genuinely open-ended tasks.
common_trap: Choosing an agent or multi-agent design because it sounds more capable. If the steps are known, a workflow is cheaper and more predictable, and if one retrieval-augmented call suffices, nothing more is needed.

title: Aligning solutions to business value pillars and SLAs
concept: Business value for Claude solutions falls into pillars, and each needs its own measurement. Efficiency: the same or better outcome with less effort, measured as time or cost per unit against a baseline. Transformation: new capabilities or markets that were not viable before. Productivity: faster delivery of useful work, measured by cycle time and quality, not output volume. Cost: total cost per correct outcome including inference, human review, escalation, evaluation, and maintenance, not tokens or per-call price. Performance SLAs: percentile latency, availability, and accuracy targets, defined on what the user or contract measures (for example, completion of the full response). Architecture choices map to these outcomes: routing by difficulty balances cost and accuracy; asynchronous batch processing lowers cost when no one is waiting; parallelizing independent calls and matching model size to step difficulty shortens latency; caching and prompt trimming reduce repeated spend. Build the business case on a measured baseline and a pilot, report net value after verification and rework, and avoid activity metrics such as usage counts, lines generated, or tokens processed. When pillars conflict (cost versus accuracy, speed versus quality), segment the workload and decide per segment.
why_it_matters: Executives fund outcomes, not architectures. Tying design decisions to a measurable pillar and an SLA lets an architect justify choices and show whether the solution delivered.
common_trap: Reporting activity or per-call cost and calling it value. A system can process more tickets and use fewer tokens while shifting cost to verification and escalation, leaving real value unchanged.

title: System prompts, templates, and guardrails
concept: A system prompt is the operator's standing contract with the model: role and scope, policies, tone, output format, and what to do at the boundaries (decline, redirect, escalate). Strong prompts state outcomes and constraints, give the reason behind important rules, say which rule wins when two collide, and define the alternative behavior rather than only a prohibition. Structure helps: separate instructions, reference material, and user input with clear headings or XML tags so they never blur. Templates insert variables such as a customer profile, retrieved documents, or user text. Treat every variable as data: wrap it in labeled tags and say it is not instructions. Keep stable text first and variable text last, which also keeps the prefix cacheable. Guardrails come in two kinds. Prompt-level guardrails (tone, scope, reading level, refusal style) are probabilistic and are validated with evals. Enforced controls (permissions, validators, output filters, schema constraints) are required for anything with security, financial, or legal consequences. Put output constraints in the contract too: nullable fields for absent values and enums with an 'other' escape beat prose instructions alone. Prompts written for older models often over-steer current ones, so audit emphasis and step-by-step choreography against an eval, and keep exact scripts only where one sequence is safe, such as a mandatory disclosure.
why_it_matters: The system prompt is the highest-leverage and most-inherited artifact in a Claude application. Prompts that grow by accretion, mix data with instructions, or carry guardrails that need code produce inconsistent behavior and security gaps that look like model problems.
common_trap: Treating a prompt rule as a control. 'Never reveal X' or 'never approve above Y' in a system prompt reduces the rate of failure but cannot guarantee it; anything with real consequences also needs enforcement in code.

title: Zero-shot, few-shot, and chain-of-thought: choosing the technique
concept: Zero-shot prompting (instructions only) is the default. With clear criteria, capable models often meet the bar, and examples add tokens and bias. Add few-shot examples when the eval shows format drift, blurry decision boundaries, or inconsistent judgments that prose cannot pin down. Examples are the strongest signal in a prompt: the model copies their length, style, and label mix. So use a small set, typically two to four, that is diverse in incidental features, spans every label, and includes borderline cases near the decision boundary, with a short reason where the choice is genuinely ambiguous. A single example gets over-copied, and examples all of one label skew the output. Examples teach how to apply judgment the model already has; they do not supply missing domain facts, which belong in context. Vague quality words such as 'be conservative' do not help; explicit criteria do. Chain-of-thought helps multi-step reasoning, rule application, and arithmetic by making intermediate steps explicit. It costs output tokens and latency and adds little to simple classification. Put the reasoning before the answer, because answer-first defeats it, keep it in separate tags or fields so code parses only the answer, and on current models prefer adaptive thinking with an effort setting to a hand-written 'think step by step'. Decide with the eval: accuracy, p95 latency, and cost per task.
why_it_matters: Each technique trades tokens, latency, and brittleness for accuracy. Choosing by evidence keeps prompts short and fast where they can be, and adds examples or reasoning only where they measurably pay.
common_trap: Adding more examples of the same kind, or a generic 'think carefully', when the real gap is an unclear boundary, a skewed example set, or missing knowledge.

title: Prompt reuse: caching, modular prompts, and Agent Skills
concept: Three mechanisms provide three kinds of reuse. Prompt caching reuses computation. The API matches a prefix in render order (tools, then system, then messages), so any byte change inside the prefix invalidates everything after it. Put stable content first (tools in a fixed order, a frozen system prompt, shared documents) and volatile content last (timestamps, user names, retrieved passages, the question). Place a cache_control breakpoint at the end of the shared portion; at most four are allowed per request. Choose the TTL by the gap between requests: 5-minute entries refresh on every read, so continuous traffic needs nothing more, while the pricier 1-hour entries fit gaps of 5 to 60 minutes. Prefixes under the model's minimum silently do not cache, caches are per model, and parallel cold requests cannot read an entry still being written. Verify with usage: compare cache reads with the sum of input, creation, and read tokens, and re-check after every prompt change. Modular prompts reuse authoring: assemble versioned components such as shared instructions, tenant policy, and per-request context, ordered by stability so modularity does not destroy cacheability. Agent Skills reuse instructions across agents without paying for them on every request: only each skill's name and description sit in context, and the full SKILL.md loads when the task calls for it.
why_it_matters: Repeated prompt text is one of the largest avoidable costs and latencies in production. Reuse done well cuts both while keeping instructions in one maintained place; done badly it silently stops working while requests still succeed.
common_trap: Adding cache_control markers and assuming caching works. A timestamp or user name early in the prompt, a tool list in unstable order, or a breakpoint after the unique tail turns every request into a pure write.

title: Choosing an observability architecture for agents at scale
concept: One user-visible outcome from an agent is the product of many model calls, tool calls, retries, and branches, often across processes and queues. Choosing an observability architecture means deciding how to reconstruct that chain affordably. Start with correlation: assign a trace ID to each run, create nested spans for every model and tool call, and propagate the context across process, queue, and subagent boundaries; without propagation, spans from workers look like unrelated traces. Use a common telemetry schema so components can be compared. Next, control volume and cost. Record lightweight metrics for all traffic, with low-cardinality labels (tool, model, release); put request and user IDs on traces and logs, not metric labels, because unbounded labels explode storage. Payload-heavy traces are expensive, so sample by rule (keep errors, slow runs, flagged runs, plus a random baseline) rather than uniformly, and consider capturing content only on demand. Attribute cost from the token usage in each response, tagged by product and feature. Treat privacy as a pipeline decision: redact or drop sensitive fields at the source or collector, before data leaves your trust boundary, export only an attribute allowlist, restrict access, and shorten retention. Finally, decide build versus buy: instrument with a vendor-neutral tracing standard and use a managed backend unless a requirement truly demands custom storage. How you then operate quality monitoring on top of this belongs to a separate objective.
why_it_matters: Without a deliberate architecture, teams either cannot reconstruct a failing run or pay for storing everything. Good choices make runs traceable, bounded in cost, and compliant from the start.
common_trap: Treating more logging as better observability: uncorrelated per-process logs, uniform sampling, or metric labels full of IDs add cost without making a failing run reconstructable.

title: Designing a RAG pipeline: chunking and indexing
concept: A RAG system is only as good as what its index can hand back, and most indexing decisions are made before any query arrives. Chunking decides the unit of retrieval. Fixed-size splitting is simple but cuts through clauses, tables, and functions; structure-aware chunking follows headings, sections, clauses, intact tables with their headers, or function boundaries, with modest overlap (not blanket 50%) to protect facts at seams. Chunk size is a trade-off: small chunks match narrow questions precisely but lose surroundings, large chunks carry context but blur the embedding and cost tokens. Small-to-big designs resolve it by matching on small chunks and returning the parent section. Context loss is the second problem: a chunk that says revenue grew 3% does not say whose. Contextual retrieval prepends a short, chunk-specific context before embedding and keyword indexing; prompt caching and a small model keep that ingestion-time cost low. Metadata (source, version, date, type, access scope) enables hard filters that similarity cannot. Finally, indexes are living systems: key chunks to a document ID and hash for incremental updates, delete superseded chunks, and never mix embedding models in one index; roll out a new model or chunker as a parallel, versioned index validated against labeled queries and switched by alias.
why_it_matters: Retrieval quality is capped by indexing choices, and fixes at query time cannot recover information that chunking destroyed. Good indexing also determines update latency, cost, and the ability to roll back.
common_trap: Compensating at query time (higher top-k, bigger model, more overlap) for a chunking or metadata flaw; it adds cost and noise without restoring what the index lost.

title: Retrieval strategies matched to data shape and query pattern
concept: There is no single best retriever; the right one depends on the shape of the data and the pattern of the queries. For prose where users paraphrase, embeddings retrieve by meaning. For literal strings such as part numbers, error codes, names, and statute citations, keyword search (BM25) is exact where embeddings blur. Mixed workloads use hybrid retrieval: run both and merge by rank, since raw scores are on different scales (reciprocal rank fusion is a common approach). Because first-stage retrieval optimizes recall and speed, a reranker can rescore a modest candidate pool (tens, not thousands) and fit the best few passages in the prompt; pool size is a latency and cost lever. Structured data is a different shape: sums, counts, and joins belong in SQL or a validated, read-only query tool, not in similarity search over rows. Small, stable corpora may not need retrieval at all: put them in context and cache them. Multi-hop questions, fast-changing sources like code, and corpora with fast-moving permissions favor agentic search, where the model issues and refines queries with search and fetch tools under a step budget and the user's own credentials, trading latency and tokens for exactness and freshness. Choose by asking what the data looks like, how queries are phrased, how often content and permissions change, and what latency and cost the use case allows.
why_it_matters: Many RAG failures are retrieval-shape mismatches, not model failures. Picking the right access path is cheaper and more reliable than tuning a single retriever to do everything.
common_trap: Defaulting to vector search for everything: embedding table rows, identifiers, or tiny stable documents adds cost and error where SQL, keyword search, or plain context would be exact.

title: Evaluating tool and agent configuration for capability bloat
concept: Capability bloat is what happens when an agent is given more tools, permissions, or reach than its job requires. It hurts in two ways. Reliability: every extra tool definition consumes context and enlarges the choice set, so selection accuracy drops, especially when tools overlap in purpose or have near-identical descriptions. Safety: every extra tool is attack surface and a way to take an action nobody intended. Evaluate a configuration by asking, per agent role, which tools the role needs, which are redundant with built-ins or with each other, and which grant more than the task requires. Remedies, in rough order of preference: remove tools the role never needs (a preventive control, stronger than prompting or confirmations); scope tools per subagent or session rather than sharing one universal set; replace broad generic tools with narrow, purpose-built ones (a validated load_document instead of a free-form fetch); split multi-mode tools into one tool per purpose; give overlapping tools distinct names and descriptions that say when to use each versus the other; and remove duplicates of built-in capabilities. When one role needs an occasional capability, give it a narrow cross-role tool rather than the whole toolset. Check non-description causes too, such as keyword bias in the system prompt. Permissions belong in the tool configuration and credentials, not in prose instructions.
why_it_matters: Tool-selection errors and over-privileged agents look like model problems but are configuration problems. Fixing them is cheaper and more reliable than adding prompt rules.
common_trap: Adding instructions, confirmation prompts, or longer descriptions on top of an over-provisioned toolset: these compensate for the excess instead of removing it.

title: Authentication and authorization gaps in Claude applications
concept: Security review of a Claude integration starts by asking whose authority each action runs under and where it is enforced. The model is not a security boundary: it can be manipulated through prompts and retrieved content, and any identifier or role it supplies is untrusted input. Authorization must therefore be enforced in code, keyed to the authenticated session, not in the system prompt or tool descriptions. Key gaps to look for: secrets in source, images, or browser bundles (use a secret manager or runtime injection, scoped per environment, rotated; if exposed, disable and replace first, then audit); a shared service identity with broad privileges behind a per-user interface, which creates a confused deputy and hides the real actor in audit logs; missing tenant isolation in conversation state, memory, caches, and retrieval (partition by authenticated tenant and user, and filter retrieval by the user's permissions before content enters context); and MCP servers shared over HTTP without endpoint authentication. Prefer delegated, per-user credentials (OAuth, token exchange) so downstream systems enforce each user's own rights, with narrow scopes, validated token audience, and short lifetimes. Give agents dedicated least-privilege roles, such as a read-only database role scoped to needed schemas. Keep a per-user audit trail from the original identity through every tool call. Compensating controls like output filters or prompt rules do not replace preventive access control.
why_it_matters: Most serious incidents in agent systems are access-control failures rather than model failures. Getting identity, scope, and isolation right limits the damage of any prompt injection or mistake.
common_trap: Putting permissions in the prompt (for example 'admins only') while every call runs under one full-privilege account; the model's compliance is not an access control.

title: Accuracy-latency-cost trade-offs and configuration choices
concept: Most configuration decisions in a Claude system move three quantities against one another: answer quality, latency, and cost. Treat each as a requirement of the use case, then pick the cheapest configuration that meets quality at the required latency, and verify with evaluations rather than intuition. Model tier: larger models are generally more capable, slower, and costlier; use the smallest tier that passes your evals, and consider routing easy requests to smaller models. Extended thinking and effort: more reasoning can raise accuracy on hard tasks but adds latency and tokens, and thinking tokens count toward the output limit, so budget for it. Retrieval depth: more passages raise recall but add tokens, latency, and distraction. Streaming improves perceived latency (time to first token) without changing total time, and suits long interactive answers. Batch processing roughly halves price for non-urgent work but has no latency guarantee, finishes within a day, and cannot run multi-turn tool loops, so it suits overnight bulk jobs, not interactive or blocking flows; submission cadence plus processing time must fit any SLA. Parallelism cuts wall-clock time for independent calls, bounded by rate limits (use a semaphore and keep retries). Timeouts and retries multiply worst-case time. Prompt caching reduces latency and cost for stable prefixes.
why_it_matters: Choosing configuration by habit leads to overspending on easy traffic or failing latency targets on interactive paths. Justifying each choice against measured requirements is what architects are asked to do.
common_trap: Assuming a latency-tolerant workload automatically fits batch, or that the largest model is the safe default; both ignore the constraints and cost of the choice.

title: Choosing an integration mechanism: MCP, API or CLI, agent-to-agent
concept: Choose the integration mechanism by who needs the capability, who owns it, and whether a model decision is involved at all. If no model judgment is needed (fixed, high-volume, deterministic calls), call the API directly from your code and use Claude only where language understanding is needed. If one application needs a capability tied to its own request context (user session, database transaction), a custom client tool in that application is simplest. If the capability must be reused across clients or applications (Claude Code, other agents, several apps), needs independent ownership and upgrades, or requires authenticated live access to a system, an MCP server fits; prefer a well-maintained community server for standard integrations and build custom only for uncovered needs. Use stdio for local, single-user servers and Streamable HTTP with authentication for shared servers that hold central credentials. If a trusted CLI is already installed and authenticated (such as gh), the Bash tool with permission rules is often the simplest option; no new server needed. Anthropic-hosted server tools, like web search, remove the need to run your own scraper. For static procedural knowledge, a Skill is better than a server. When the other party is an autonomous agent with its own tools, memory, and lifecycle, treat it as a peer service: a versioned task-oriented contract with asynchronous status and results, not a bag of its internal tools. Wrapping every integration in MCP, or reimplementing built-ins, adds cost without value.
why_it_matters: The wrong mechanism creates duplicated code, security gaps, or needless model calls. Matching mechanism to reuse, ownership, and decision needs keeps systems simple and secure.
common_trap: Defaulting to MCP for everything, including one-app tools, deterministic pipeline calls, and static guidance that a Skill or plain code would handle better.

title: Progressive discovery versus monolithic context
concept: Context is a finite, costly resource: everything loaded up front consumes tokens, adds latency, and competes for the model's attention. Progressive discovery loads information only when a task needs it. Common forms are Skills (only name and description sit in context until the Skill is used), on-demand tool discovery (core tools loaded, others found via a tool-search mechanism), path-scoped rules and subdirectory instruction files that load when that area is touched, and just-in-time retrieval, where the agent holds lightweight references and fetches detail through layered tools (search returns summaries and IDs, a second call returns a section). The monolithic alternative puts everything in the system prompt or tool list, which is simple and deterministic. Choose by relevance and criticality. Use progressive loading when most content is irrelevant to most requests, the library is large or growing, or tool counts degrade selection. Keep content always loaded when it applies to every request, is small, or must never be missed (mandatory rules); critical checks can also be enforced in code. Progressive loading has costs: extra round trips, and discoverability depends on good descriptions because the model decides what to load. Avoid changing the tools list per turn, which breaks prompt-cache prefixes; prefer a stable prefix plus discovery.
why_it_matters: Loading everything wastes tokens and degrades accuracy as capabilities grow, while lazy-loading everything risks missed rules and extra latency. The architect's task is to place each piece of context deliberately.
common_trap: Treating progressive discovery as universally better; for small, always-needed, or mandatory content a static, cached prefix is cheaper and more reliable.

title: Defining evaluation metrics for a Claude application
concept:
A metric is useful only if it is measurable, tied to the use case's success criterion, and sensitive to the failures that matter. Start from the business outcome and derive metrics per dimension: accuracy or faithfulness (task-specific: claim-level support for summaries, per-class precision and recall for classification, field-level accuracy for extraction), latency (time to first token and percentiles for interactive channels, end-to-end completion for batch), cost (per completed task, including retries and extra turns, not per request), safety (harmful or unsupported output rate, severity-weighted), and security (attack success rate on a maintained adversarial set, paired with benign refusal rate).

Four design rules recur. First, disaggregate: an aggregate is volume-weighted, so report by segment and by severity, and weight metrics by the cost of each error type. Second, pair metrics so that no single number can be improved by degrading something else: a primary metric plus guardrails with agreed thresholds. Third, prefer outcome metrics over proxies (overlap scores, length, judge scores) or validate any proxy against human ratings. Fourth, define thresholds and the measurement protocol before running the evaluation, so the same procedure can gate every later change. Measured values then feed eval datasets (4.2), comparisons (4.3), and production monitoring (4.6).
why_it_matters: Metrics decide what the team optimizes. A convenient but misaligned metric produces a system that scores well and fails users, and aggregate numbers can hide the segments where the risk concentrates.
common_trap: Reporting one aggregate or proxy number (overall accuracy, average latency, a judge score) and treating it as the success criterion; it can rise while the failures that matter get worse.

title: Designing evaluation datasets and test frameworks
concept:
An evaluation framework has three parts: a dataset, graders, and a run protocol. The dataset (a golden set) should mirror the production input distribution, add rare types and known failure cases, carry trusted human labels, and be held out from prompt tuning so scores generalize. Grow it continuously by adding failures found in production, which turns each incident into a permanent regression case.

Choose the grader per criterion. Code-based graders (schema validation, exact or numeric match, assertions that forbidden actions did not occur, final-state checks for agents) are cheap, exact, and deterministic. LLM-as-judge handles subjective properties such as tone or completeness; it needs a rubric, validation against human labels, and controls for known biases (position and length). Human grading is the highest-fidelity and most expensive, so use it to create labels, calibrate judges, and audit samples rather than on every run. Mixed methodologies are normal: one case may carry code checks and a judged rubric.

Because output is non-deterministic, grade properties instead of exact strings, run cases several times when variance matters, and track pass rates rather than single outcomes. Wire the suite into CI as a regression gate for every prompt, model, or tooling change, with thresholds agreed beforehand.
why_it_matters: A trustworthy evaluation suite is what lets a team change prompts and models with confidence. Without one, quality is judged by anecdote, and regressions reach users before anyone notices.
common_trap: Building the dataset from easy hand-picked examples, or from the model's own output, and letting tuning examples leak into the test set; scores then rise without real-world improvement.

title: A/B testing and iterative improvement for Claude systems
concept:
Improvement should be an experiment loop: form a hypothesis, change one thing, measure against a fixed evaluation set, and only then compare in production. Offline, run the candidate against the regression suite so that a fix for one failure does not break another. Online, use a controlled comparison: randomize concurrent traffic across arms (by the unit that experiences the treatment, such as the user), hold the model, prompt, retrieval index, and settings constant except for the factor under test, and judge a pre-chosen primary metric with guardrails for latency, cost, and safety.

Statistical discipline matters. Fix the sample size beforehand from the baseline rate and the smallest effect worth detecting; run complete weekly cycles; avoid stopping at the first significant look; and treat post-hoc subgroup wins as hypotheses for a follow-up test because many slices produce chance results.

Rollout techniques manage risk rather than measure effect. Shadow mode runs the candidate on live inputs with outputs logged but never shown, and must intercept side-effecting tool calls. A canary exposes a small real share with predefined rollback thresholds, then widens in stages. Keep the previous prompt and model ID versioned so that rollback is a configuration revert.
why_it_matters: Prompt and model changes often move quality in unexpected directions. Controlled comparison turns opinion into evidence and keeps regressions from reaching all users at once.
common_trap: Comparing this week to last week, bundling several changes into one arm, or declaring a winner from a small or repeatedly peeked sample.

title: Diagnosing prompt failures, hallucinations, and model mismatch
concept:
Diagnosis moves from symptoms to cause by narrowing the layer at fault. Start with the cheapest checks: integration (stop_reason of max_tokens, 4xx request errors, dropped or unflagged tool results, stale or incomplete input), then see whether the information the model needed was actually present in its context. If it was not, fix the pipeline (retrieval, input assembly) rather than the prompt. If it was present, inspect the prompt for contradictory or ambiguous instructions, for critical instructions placed far from the point of generation in long inputs, and for missing output constraints.

Hallucinations come in two kinds: fabrication when information is absent (give the model a legitimate way to say so, such as nullable fields or abstention, and verify claims against sources) and misgrounding when the information is present but ignored (require quoted evidence, check it mechanically). Model mismatch shows as failures concentrated in the hardest cases after a model change or downgrade; confirm it by running the same eval across models and across prompt versions, separating prompt effects from capability limits.

Use evidence at each step: a failure taxonomy from sampled errors, paired comparisons that change one variable, and traces that show what the model saw. Prefer fixes at the layer that caused the failure over compensating controls such as prompt warnings.
why_it_matters: Treating a retrieval, input, or integration fault as a model or prompt problem wastes cost and can make the system worse. Layered diagnosis finds the actual cause and prevents repeated incidents.
common_trap: Jumping to a bigger model, a lower temperature, or a 'never make things up' prompt line before checking what the model was actually given and what the response metadata showed.

title: Optimizing tokens, latency, and cost-performance trade-offs
concept:
Cost and latency come from three places: input tokens, output (and reasoning) tokens, and the model chosen. Apply levers in order of risk. Free wins change nothing about quality: prompt caching (stable content first, volatile content after the breakpoint; cache reads cost a fraction of normal input, writes a small premium; the default lifetime is short, with a longer option for sporadic traffic; caches are scoped per model and workspace), trimming redundant prompt content, and the Message Batches API for non-urgent work (about half price, results within 24 hours, no latency guarantee, matched by custom_id).

Quality-trading levers need evaluation: lower effort on routine or high-volume routes, shape output length with instructions or structured output (output tokens are the slow and expensive part; max_tokens is a safety cap, not a length control), and route simple requests to smaller models while keeping complex ones on larger models. Measure each against a quality floor on the eval set and adopt only what holds. Latency has its own levers: streaming improves perceived latency, effort and output length cut real generation time, and premium faster-output options carry a price premium.

Compare options by cost per completed task, including retries and extra turns, and use the usage fields (input, cache write, cache read, output) to see where the money goes.
why_it_matters: Production bills and response times scale with traffic. Choosing levers in the right order cuts spend without trading away quality the business depends on.
common_trap: Truncating with a small max_tokens, switching everything to the cheapest model, or batching an interactive workload; each saves per-request cost by degrading the result.

title: Monitoring production Claude systems with logs and observability
concept:
Operating a Claude application means watching service health and answer quality, because an LLM system can fail silently while returning valid responses. Instrumentation design (what to log, where to redact, how to sample and retain) is an architecture decision covered under 3.4; here the focus is what to watch and act on once it exists.

Monitor four signal families. Reliability: the user-visible failure rate after retries, the error mix by status code (429, 529, 5xx, 400), and the stop_reason distribution; a rising max_tokens share signals truncation. Performance and cost: percentile latency, time to first token, cache hit rate, and cost per completed task. Quality: a stratified random sample of production outputs scored per segment by validated graders and human review, since aggregates hide weak segments. Drift: input mix over time, so a new language, product line, or template is noticed before complaints arrive, together with a fixed golden set rerun periodically to separate input drift from a change in the system.

Alert on service-level indicators over windows, with an owner and a runbook, instead of paging on every transient error, to avoid fatigue. After every prompt or model change, compare the new version's sampled quality and feedback with the baseline and alert on a drop beyond an agreed margin. Capture user and reviewer feedback keyed to the trace ID, and feed confirmed failures into the regression set and prompt improvements.
why_it_matters: Silent regressions reach users long before aggregate dashboards move. Good observability shortens detection, narrows the cause, and turns each incident into a permanent test.
common_trap: Watching only latency and error rates; a model that returns fluent but wrong answers looks healthy on those dashboards while quality degrades.

title: LLM risks, limitations, and failure modes
concept: An architect treats an LLM component as a powerful but fallible and probabilistic part of a larger system. The main failure modes are: hallucination, where the model produces fluent text that is not grounded in facts or sources; prompt injection and data leakage, where untrusted content steers the model or context is disclosed; overreliance, where humans stop checking output because it is usually right; non-determinism, where identical inputs can produce different outputs and model upgrades change behavior; and error propagation, where a wrong early output is treated as truth by later stages. Structured outputs remove syntax errors but not semantic ones, such as totals that do not sum, and a schema that forces a value invites fabrication when the source lacks it. Controls follow the failure: ground answers in retrieved sources and require quotes, allow null or unknown, validate at stage boundaries against source and rules, record decisions with inputs and versions instead of relying on replay, and design human review that actually verifies. Distinguish an access failure from a genuine empty result so an outage is never reported as no findings.
why_it_matters: Most production incidents come from a plausible but wrong output moving through a system unchecked. Naming the failure mode points to a preventive control in the architecture instead of a hopeful prompt change.
common_trap: Believing a larger model, lower randomness, or a stern prompt instruction removes a failure mode. They reduce its rate but cannot guarantee its absence, so high-stakes paths still need validation and review.

title: Human-in-the-loop validation strategies
concept: Human oversight is a scarce resource, so design it deliberately. Start by classifying actions and outputs by consequence: reversibility, financial or safety impact, and legal exposure. Low-risk, reversible work runs automatically; irreversible or high-impact actions pass through an approval gate enforced in the execution layer, so the agent cannot bypass it. For review of outputs, route by risk rather than by volume: send low-calibrated-confidence or contradictory cases to people, auto-approve the well-measured remainder, and keep a stratified random sample of auto-approved items to estimate true error rates and catch drift. Raw self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and must be checked against labeled data before it gates anything. Escalation triggers should be explicit: a customer asks for a human, policy is silent or requires an exception, or the agent cannot make progress; sentiment is not a reliable trigger. Give reviewers what they need to decide quickly: a concise summary, the evidence, risk flags, and a recommended action. Gates that fire too often cause approval fatigue and become rubber stamps.
why_it_matters: Human review is the last line of defense for consequential decisions, but it only works if it is targeted, informed, and enforced by the system. Poorly designed oversight adds cost without adding safety.
common_trap: Gating on the model's own confidence or sentiment, or sending everything to approval. The first misroutes in both directions; the second trains reviewers to approve without reading.

title: Regulatory compliance at an architect's level
concept: Compliance work starts by identifying which regulations apply to the data and the use, then turning each into design constraints. For GDPR, the recurring ones are lawful basis and purpose limitation, data minimization, storage limitation, data-subject rights including access and erasure, and restrictions on cross-border transfer, so residency applies to every copy of personal data: prompts, outputs, logs, caches, and vector stores. For HIPAA, protected health information is generally shared with a vendor only under a business associate agreement that covers the specific service, and only the minimum necessary should be sent; audit controls must record who accessed what and when, with purpose captured where policy requires it. For FedRAMP, federal data at a given impact level generally must run in a service and boundary authorized at that level, and authorization is scoped to specific services, not to a provider as a whole. In practice: minimize and pseudonymize before prompting, choose a deployment path that holds the required authorization or agreement, key stored data by subject so it can be deleted, keep structured audit trails at the tool layer, and verify claims with the vendor instead of assuming them.
why_it_matters: A design that ignores a legal constraint may have to be rebuilt after launch, or may expose the organization to liability. Raising these constraints during requirements is far cheaper than discovering them in review.
common_trap: Treating compliance as a prompt instruction, a redaction step, or a vendor's general reputation. Obligations attach to data flows, agreements, and authorization scope, which the architecture must enforce and verify.

title: Ethical AI: bias, fairness, and transparency
concept: Ethical design is a set of testable engineering practices. For bias, evaluate behavior instead of trusting intent: run matched-pair tests that change only a demographic signal, compute outcome and error rates by group on realistic data, and repeat after changes to prompts, models, or data. Removing protected attributes is not enough, because proxies and historical labels carry bias, and dropping demographic data from evaluation only hides disparities. Fairness has several competing definitions, such as equal selection rates versus equal error rates, so choose the criterion deliberately with legal and business stakeholders and document the trade-off. Check that examples and ground truth reflect job-relevant criteria, not past biased decisions. For transparency, disclose when users are dealing with an AI, answer truthfully if asked, give reasons based on the factors actually used rather than post-hoc rationales, and show sources so users can verify. For consequential decisions, provide human review and a way to appeal. Monitor outcomes by group in production and have a response plan: measure the disparity, limit harm with interim review, fix, and add cases to regression tests.
why_it_matters: Unfair or opaque systems harm people and expose organizations to legal and reputational risk. Aggregates hide unequal performance, so only segment-level measurement shows who is being underserved.
common_trap: Declaring a system fair because it is equally accurate overall, because protected attributes were removed, or because a prompt tells the model to be unbiased. None of these is evidence about outcomes.

title: Communicating architectural decisions and trade-offs to different audiences
concept: Architects communicate a decision, not a design tour. The decision, its alternatives, and its trade-offs are the same for everyone; emphasis and detail change by audience. Executives need the recommendation, the decision requested, and cost, risk, and time for each real option. Security reviewers need data-flow diagrams showing what reaches the model, trust boundaries, storage and retention, and the controls at each point. Legal needs an honest account of limitations and the controls that bound their consequences. Engineers need interfaces, failure modes, and the alternatives that were rejected. Use measured evidence from the evaluation set and pilot in place of adjectives, and report distributions and categories, not only averages: a strong overall score can hide a weak category, and a routed design can hide a slow tail. Record significant decisions in architecture decision records covering context, options, decision, consequences accepted, and conditions for revisiting; when a decision changes, write a superseding record instead of editing the old one so the history survives. State residual risk and known limits plainly, including what the system will get wrong, and who accepted the risk. When tailoring, check that no audience hears a different story than another, because stakeholders compare notes.
why_it_matters: Decisions about Claude systems involve uncertainty that stakeholders cannot see unless the architect shows it. Honest, audience-appropriate communication earns approvals that hold up, and a decision record lets successors understand and safely change the design.
common_trap: Selling the design: leading with benefits, quoting a blended average, or giving each audience a different emphasis. Trust is lost when a stakeholder later finds the omitted limitation or compares briefings.

title: Aligning expectations: SLAs, SLOs, and feedback loops for probabilistic systems
concept: Stakeholders expect software to be deterministic, but Claude-based systems are probabilistic: wording varies, some answers are wrong, and quality depends on the input mix. Expectation management starts by replacing absolute promises with measurable service objectives. For quality, define the population, the sampling method, the grading rubric (often severity-weighted by question class), and the window; measure it on sampled production traffic, not only on a curated set. For latency, use percentiles, and for streamed output use time to first token separately from total completion time. For availability, commit only to what the dependency chain supports, include a graceful fallback in the definition of a valid response, and show how upstream outages consume the error budget. Consistency should be defined by outcomes (same decision or facts), not identical text. Calibrate targets on production-representative data, because pilot results on clean inputs overstate performance. Pair objectives with leading indicators and a review cadence that triggers re-scoping. Feedback closes the loop: capture ratings, edits, and overrides; classify them by reason; add representative cases to the evaluation set; name a single owner and rubric for conflicting requests; and ship changes through a gated, versioned release. Include a change-management commitment for model retirements: notice, evaluation, rollback, and regression thresholds.
why_it_matters: Most disputes over AI systems stem from unmatched expectations, not defects. Agreeing how quality, latency, and change will be measured up front lets stakeholders judge the system fairly and gives the team a legitimate route to improve it.
common_trap: Signing a single headline SLA (such as 99 percent accuracy) with no measurement definition, or relying on pilot figures from curated data. The first dispute then turns on what the number meant.

title: Documenting architectures and guiding the teams that implement and operate them
concept: Documentation for a Claude system serves different readers and must capture what is unusual about it: behavior is shaped by prompts, tool definitions, retrieval content, and model choice, and these change without code changing. Architecture documentation should include data-flow and sequence diagrams that show trust boundaries and the error, timeout, and fallback paths, plus decision records that explain why the design was chosen. Runbooks are for operators under pressure: entries are keyed to symptoms (rate-limit errors, truncated output, schema failures, cost spikes, quality regressions) and give diagnostic steps, owners, and rollback procedures for versioned prompt and model configuration. A handoff pack adds the evaluation set with baseline scores and instructions for running it, cost and token assumptions, known limitations with escalation paths, and a supervised first change by the receiving team. Implementation guidance, such as an add-a-source playbook or a local-run guide using a mocked client and recorded fixtures, encodes lessons so teams can extend the system safely. Because wording varies, express acceptance criteria as thresholds over an evaluation set with exact checks only for structured fields. Keep prompts and tool definitions versioned in the repository with the reason for non-obvious instructions, so documentation does not drift from behavior. For regulated settings, record the model, prompt version, retrieved documents, and tool calls that produced each answer.
why_it_matters: Teams that inherit a Claude system cannot see why it behaves as it does from the code alone. Good documentation lets them diagnose incidents, change prompts and sources safely, and answer auditors without relying on the original authors.
common_trap: Handing over a long design document and treating it as the handoff. Operators need symptom-keyed runbooks, a working evaluation harness, and practice with a supervised change; prose descriptions of intent do not provide them.

title: Structured discovery for Claude solutions
concept: Discovery decides whether a Claude solution is feasible and what it must achieve, so it should be structured rather than a collection of conversations with the sponsor. Start with the business outcome and turn vague goals into measurable targets with a measured baseline: handle time, error rate, cost per transaction. Define what a correct output means for this domain and who judges it, because that definition becomes the evaluation set. Map the stakeholders beyond the sponsor: the people who do the work, QA, owners of downstream systems, and security, privacy, legal, and compliance, since their constraints are requirements. Investigate data availability early: where the data lives, its formats and quality, freshness, ownership, access permissions, and whether labeled examples exist; test on a representative sample that includes the worst inputs. Capture non-functional requirements such as throughput, latency, availability, residency, and cost ceilings, and note where platform and region choices limit model and feature availability. Establish the cost of a wrong answer by question type, because it drives review and escalation. When stakeholders conflict, look for the underlying need, often two jobs in one brief, and make the trade-off an explicit decision with sign-off. Output of discovery is a requirements set with measurable criteria, a data and feasibility assessment, and a list of open risks.
why_it_matters: Most failed AI projects fail on data, scope, or unmeasured success criteria that discovery could have exposed. Time spent here is much cheaper than rework after an architecture has been built around a wrong assumption.
common_trap: Taking the sponsor's description at face value: clean data, a tolerance for errors, and a vague goal such as accurate or faster. Verify each on real samples and with the people who use the output.

title: AI-assisted developer workflows: plan mode, CI automation, and review at team scale
concept: Workflow improvements come from matching the mode of working to the task and keeping controls where risk is. Use plan mode when scope is large, several approaches are viable, or design decisions precede edits (multi-file migrations, architectural choices); use direct execution when the change is well-scoped, and switch from plan to execution once the plan is approved. Escape hatches matter: if a small task reveals real design implications, step back to planning. For automation, run Claude Code non-interactively with `claude -p`, request structured output with `--output-format json` and `--json-schema`, and have the CI step parse the structured findings and set the check status itself (exit non-zero on critical ones), since `claude -p` exits non-zero when the run fails, not when it finds problems. Scope what an unattended run may do preventively, with a narrow allowlist and a restrictive permission mode such as `dontAsk`, rather than detectively. Be aware that a plain `-p` run in a checkout loads that repository's project hooks and MCP servers without a trust dialog; for CI over untrusted code, `--bare` plus pipeline-controlled configuration avoids this. For code review, use an independent instance rather than the generating session, pass prior findings to prevent duplicates, write precision-oriented criteria, and disable noisy categories rather than let them erode trust in good ones. AI-drafted changes keep the same gates: tests, independent review, and human approval.
why_it_matters: Productivity gains disappear if the bot is noisy, unsafe, or bypasses existing quality gates. Architects choose the workflow and controls so speed does not come at the cost of trust or security.
common_trap: Granting broad permissions because the runner is ephemeral, or letting the generating session review its own work. Both trade a preventive or independent control for convenience.

code_samples.caption: Unattended CI run with narrow, preventive scoping and structured output
code_samples.code:
# --bare does not read OAuth or the keychain: set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY (or an apiKeyHelper)
claude --bare -p "Review this diff against the attached criteria" \
  --append-system-prompt-file ci/review-criteria.md \
  --permission-mode dontAsk \
  --allowedTools "Read,Bash(git diff *)" \
  --output-format json --json-schema "$(cat ci/findings.schema.json)" > review.json
# the CI step, not Claude, decides the status
jq -e '[.structured_output.findings[] | select(.severity=="critical")] | length == 0' review.json

title: Debugging and operating Claude-powered systems: triage, replay, and rollback
concept: Two skills sit under this objective: using Claude to speed up incident and debugging work, and debugging Claude-powered systems that are running in production. When using Claude for triage, give it focused evidence (the incident window, error lines, request IDs, the recent deploy or config diff), ask for ranked hypotheses that cite supporting evidence, and verify each before acting. Keep investigation access read-only and enforced by permissions and credentials, not by instructions; remediation is a separate, reviewed step. When a Claude-powered system misbehaves, separate integration causes from model behavior: check stop_reason (truncation), the request actually sent, tool_result handling, error class, and prompt and model versions before blaming the model. Contain first: roll back the last prompt or model change through the pipeline, then reproduce. Reproduction needs captured inputs, versions, response metadata, and tool calls, correlated by request ID and redacted for sensitive data. Replaying failures against old and new versions isolates what changed. Retry only transient errors, keep one retry layer, and treat repeated tool loops or cost spikes as signals to read traces.
why_it_matters: Incidents in probabilistic systems are hard to reproduce, so the evidence you captured beforehand decides how fast you recover. Containment and preventive access control limit damage while you diagnose.
common_trap: Tuning temperature, adding retries, or editing prompts live to make a symptom disappear, instead of rolling back and diagnosing with captured evidence.
